sets.title: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Initial assessment & risk
texts.body:
Acute upper GI bleeding (AUGIB) presents with haematemesis, melaena, or both. Syncope, resting tachycardia, or postural hypotension suggest significant volume loss.

Immediate priorities
• Protect airway if ongoing massive haematemesis or reduced consciousness
• Two large-bore IV cannulae; send FBC, urea/electrolytes, coagulation, group and save (cross-match if unstable)
• Restrictive transfusion threshold usually haemoglobin <70 g/L in otherwise stable patients without cardiovascular ischaemia; higher targets may apply in ischaemic heart disease

Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) — outpatient pathway
A GBS of 0 identifies very-low-risk patients who may be considered for early discharge with urgent outpatient endoscopy rather than admission, provided social support and follow-up are reliable.

Rockall score (post-endoscopy)
Combines age, shock, comorbidity and endoscopic stigmata to estimate rebleeding and mortality risk. Do not use Rockall alone to decide pre-endoscopy triage.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Resuscitation & medical therapy algorithm
texts.body:
Step 1 — ABC and volume
Crystalloid bolus if hypotensive. Avoid over-transfusion in variceal disease (target Hb often ~70–80 g/L) because excess volume may increase portal pressure.

Step 2 — Reverse coagulopathy when indicated
• Stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants after senior discussion; do not reverse aspirin routinely before endoscopy if cardiac stents are recent — involve cardiology
• For warfarin with active major bleed: vitamin K IV + PCC as per local protocol
• DOAC major bleed: specific reversal agents where available; otherwise PCC per haematology advice

Step 3 — Acid suppression & vasoactive drugs
• Non-variceal: high-dose PPI infusion after endoscopic haemostasis (e.g. continuous omeprazole/pantoprazole infusion for 72 hours in high-risk stigmata). Pre-endoscopy PPI may be given but does not replace timely endoscopy.
• Suspected variceal bleed: start terlipressin (or octreotide if terlipressin unavailable) AND prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. IV ceftriaxone) before endoscopy.

Step 4 — Escalate early
Massive transfusion protocol if ongoing instability. Contact gastroenterology and ICU early for unstable patients.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Endoscopy timing & findings checklist
texts.body:
Timing (door-to-endoscopy guidance)
• Immediate (as soon as resuscitated): ongoing haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation, suspected variceal bleed with instability
• Within 24 hours: most admitted AUGIB patients once adequately resuscitated
• Very low risk (GBS 0): may defer to urgent outpatient slot within days if local pathway allows

Pre-endoscopy checklist
• Informed consent / capacity assessment
• NBM status documented; airway risk discussed with anaesthesia if GCS reduced
• Erythromycin IV 30–60 minutes pre-procedure may improve mucosal views in selected cases (local protocol)

High-risk endoscopic stigmata (non-variceal)
Active spurting/oozing, non-bleeding visible vessel, adherent clot — these usually need endoscopic therapy and post-procedure high-dose PPI.

Failure of endoscopic control
Arrange interventional radiology (embolisation) or surgery after joint discussion; do not delay transfer while repeating ineffective endoscopy cycles.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Post-endoscopy care & discharge criteria
texts.body:
Monitoring
• Hourly observations initially if high-risk stigmata treated; step down when stable
• Clear fluid then diet as directed by endoscopist; record any recurrent melaena/haematemesis on fluid chart

Medication plan
• Continue PPI orally after IV course completes, typically 4–8 weeks depending on ulcer pathology and H. pylori status
• Test for H. pylori (biopsy or urea breath/stool antigen when appropriate); treat if positive
• Restart necessary antithrombotics at the earliest safe interval agreed by gastroenterology/cardiology — often within 1–3 days for aspirin after haemostasis, longer for anticoagulants

Discharge only if ALL met
• Haemodynamically stable ≥24 hours after therapy
• Haemoglobin stable on two consecutive checks
• Tolerating oral intake
• Clear safety-net advice given (return if black stool, vomiting blood, dizziness, syncope)
• Follow-up endoscopy booked when indicated (e.g. gastric ulcer to exclude malignancy)

sets.title: Neutropenic sepsis pathway
sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Definitions & immediate red flags
texts.body:
Neutropenic sepsis is a time-critical emergency. Treat suspected cases before neutrophil count returns if clinical suspicion is high.

Working definitions (adult)
• Neutropenia: absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <1.0 × 10⁹/L (some protocols use <0.5 × 10⁹/L for ‘profound’)
• Fever: single oral temperature ≥38.3°C OR ≥38.0°C sustained for 1 hour
• Suspected neutropenic sepsis: fever OR other signs of infection in a patient at risk (recent chemotherapy, known haematological malignancy, stem-cell transplant) even if ANC not yet available

Red flags requiring immediate escalation
• Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg or drop ≥40 mmHg from baseline)
• Respiratory rate ≥25/min or new oxygen requirement
• Altered mental state
• Rigors with unstable observations
• Suspected source requiring source control (e.g. line infection with septic shock)

Do not wait for laboratory confirmation of neutropenia before giving the first antibiotic dose if the patient is at risk and septic.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Door-to-needle pathway (first hour)
texts.body:
Time targets from arrival / recognition
0–15 minutes
• Alert: ‘neutropenic sepsis pathway’
• ABC assessment; high-flow oxygen if SpO₂ <94% (or target per COPD protocol)
• IV access ×2; blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics whenever this does not delay therapy >15 minutes total

By 60 minutes (door-to-needle)
• First broad-spectrum IV antibiotic administered — commonly piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) as monotherapy if no penicillin allergy; alternatives per local antibiogram (e.g. meropenem if indicated)
• Lactate, FBC, U&E, CRP, clotting, group and save
• Fluid challenge if hypotensive (crystalloid 500 mL rapid bolus, reassess; repeat as needed while arranging critical care review)

Cultures & samples
• Peripheral blood cultures ± paired from central line hubs if line present
• Mid-stream urine if possible; swab any wounds; CXR if respiratory signs
• Do not delay antibiotics for imaging

If penicillin anaphylaxis history
Use locally approved non-penicillin regimen (e.g. ciprofloxacin + vancomycin — only if listed in your trust guideline).

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Risk stratification & ongoing antibiotics
texts.body:
MASCC risk index (selected low-risk outpatient pathways)
Higher MASCC scores indicate lower risk of complications. Only use outpatient oral therapy if ALL of the following apply per local policy: haemodynamically stable, no organ failure, reliable social support, able to tolerate oral medication, and MASCC high (commonly ≥21). Most inpatient oncology pathways still admit for IV therapy initially.

IV catheter / line suspected
• Examine exit site; if tunnel infection or septic shock with likely line source, discuss line removal with oncology/microbiology early
• Add vancomycin (or teicoplanin) when MRSA risk, severe mucositis, or suspected catheter-related infection — follow local dosing/levels

Reassessment at 48 hours
• If cultures negative, afebrile, and recovering neutrophils, consider de-escalation
• Persistently febrile after 72–96 hours: review for fungal infection, occult source, and discuss antifungal strategy with haematology/ID

G-CSF
Not routinely required for every febrile neutropenic episode; consider when profound neutropenia with high-risk features per oncology advice.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Patient information & discharge safety-netting
texts.body:
Education before chemotherapy discharge
Give written advice to present IMMEDIATELY if:
• Temperature ≥38.0°C
• Uncontrolled shivering/rigors
• Flu-like illness, new cough, shortness of breath
• Burning urine, diarrhoea with fever, severe mucositis preventing intake
• Dizziness, confusion, or feeling ‘the worst ever’

Home pack (where commissioned)
Some services provide emergency oral antibiotics to start after phone triage — patients must still attend for assessment the same day unless a formal telemedicine pathway confirms low risk.

After inpatient treatment — discharge criteria
• Afebrile ≥24 hours on appropriate therapy
• Clinically stable; ANC recovering or infection controlled
• Oral route reliable; follow-up bloods/clinic booked
• Clear advice on central-line care if discharged with a line

Documentation must record time of first antibiotic dose (door-to-needle) for audit.

sets.title: Peri-operative anticoagulation bridging
sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Who needs bridging? Risk categories
texts.body:
Bridging = temporary use of short-acting anticoagulant (usually LMWH) when a vitamin-K antagonist (VKA) such as warfarin is interrupted for a procedure.

Higher thromboembolic risk (bridging more often considered)
• Mechanical mitral valve OR older-generation mechanical aortic valve
• AF with prior stroke/TIA and CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥5 (local cut-offs vary)
• VTE within the preceding 3 months
• Previous VTE during interruption of anticoagulation

Lower risk (bridging often unnecessary)
• Uncomplicated AF with lower CHA₂DS₂-VASc
• Remote VTE >12 months ago and no thrombophilia
• Bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without other risk factors (many guidelines advise against routine bridging)

DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)
Usually stopped for a procedure-specific interval based on renal function and bleeding risk; routine LMWH bridging is NOT recommended for DOACs.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Warfarin interruption timetable
texts.body:
Standard elective procedure (therapeutic INR 2.0–3.0)
• Last warfarin dose: 5 days before procedure (i.e. hold for 5 doses) in most adults
• Check INR the day before surgery; if INR >1.5, consider low-dose oral vitamin K per protocol and recheck
• Target pre-op INR usually ≤1.5 for surgery with bleeding risk (specialty-specific exceptions exist)

High bleeding-risk procedures (examples)
Neuraxial anaesthesia, major cancer surgery, prostate/bladder resection, intracranial/spinal surgery — require longer clean anticoagulant windows and stricter INR targets.

Restart warfarin
• Evening of surgery or day 1 if haemostasis secure, at usual maintenance dose (± bridging overlap until INR therapeutic)
• Do not ‘load’ with large unexpected doses without senior/haematology input

texts.label: C
texts.heading: LMWH bridging doses & holding rules
texts.body:
When bridging is indicated (VKA patients)
• Start therapeutic LMWH when INR falls below therapeutic range (often ~36–48 hours after last warfarin), e.g. enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC twice daily OR 1.5 mg/kg once daily (prefer BD in higher-risk; adjust for CrCl <30 mL/min)

Hold LMWH before procedure
• Last therapeutic dose: 24 hours before surgery for twice-daily regimens
• For once-daily therapeutic regimens: give half the dose the morning before surgery, then hold
• Prophylactic-dose LMWH (if used instead of therapeutic bridging): last dose ≥12 hours pre-op

Post-procedure restart
• Prophylactic LMWH ≥12 hours after surgery if haemostasis OK
• Therapeutic LMWH usually delayed 48–72 hours after high bleeding-risk surgery
• Overlap LMWH with warfarin until INR ≥2.0 for two consecutive days (or per valve clinic target)

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Neuraxial anaesthesia & emergency surgery notes
texts.body:
Neuraxial block (spinal/epidural) — minimum intervals after LMWH
• Prophylactic enoxaparin: wait ≥12 hours after last dose before needle placement
• Therapeutic enoxaparin: wait ≥24 hours
• After catheter removal: wait ≥4 hours before next LMWH dose (local anaesthetic protocols may be stricter)

Emergency surgery on warfarin
• Discuss bleeding vs thrombosis risk with surgeon/anaesthetist/haematology
• For immediate reversal: IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC (dose by INR/weight per protocol); FFP is second-line if PCC unavailable
• Document indication, products given, and post-reversal INR

Emergency surgery on DOAC
• Record last dose time and renal function
• Delay surgery if safe; if not, consider specific reversal (e.g. idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet where available for factor-Xa inhibitors) or PCC per haematology

sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: CURB-65 severity assessment
texts.body:
One point is assigned for each of the following criteria:
• Confusion (new onset; Abbreviated Mental Test Score ≤8, or new disorientation in person, place, or time)
• Urea >7 mmol/L
• Respiratory rate ≥30 breaths/min
• Blood pressure: systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg
• Age ≥65 years

Score interpretation
• 0–1: low severity — consider home treatment with oral antibiotics if social circumstances are safe
• 2: moderate severity — consider hospital admission for supervised assessment and treatment
• 3–5: high severity — urgent hospital admission required; consider ICU assessment if score 4–5

CURB-65 guides but does not replace clinical judgement. A score of 0 or 1 does not preclude admission if the patient is hypoxic, unable to take oral medication, or lacks adequate home support. Reassess all patients within 24 hours if there is any clinical deterioration.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Empirical antibiotic therapy
texts.body:
Low severity (CURB-65 0–1)
• First choice: amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 5 days
• Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 500 mg orally twice daily for 5 days

Moderate severity (CURB-65 2)
• First choice: amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily plus clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily (both oral) for 5 days
• Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg once daily for 5 days

High severity (CURB-65 3–5)
• First choice: co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV three times daily plus clarithromycin 500 mg IV twice daily
• Penicillin allergy: levofloxacin 500 mg IV twice daily; seek microbiology advice if atypical organism suspected
• Switch to oral therapy when apyrexial for ≥24 hours, tolerating diet, and clinically improving; total course 7–10 days

Always send blood cultures before starting IV antibiotics. Review culture results at 48–72 hours and de-escalate to narrower-spectrum agents where culture and sensitivity permit.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Investigations and oxygen targets
texts.body:
All patients
• Chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis and document the extent of consolidation
• Full blood count, C-reactive protein, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, blood glucose
• Pulse oximetry on arrival; repeat at least every 4 hours until readings are stable

Moderate or severe CAP (CURB-65 ≥2)
• Two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics are given
• Sputum Gram stain and culture if purulent sputum is produced
• Urinary pneumococcal antigen test (send regardless of prior antibiotic exposure)
• Urinary Legionella antigen if cluster, recent travel, or CURB-65 ≥3
• Arterial blood gas if SpO₂ <94% or clinical respiratory failure is suspected

Oxygen therapy targets
Aim for SpO₂ 94–98% in most patients. Use a lower target of 88–92% in patients known or suspected to be at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD or neuromuscular disease). Document the target on the oxygen prescription and reassess every 30 minutes until the patient is stable.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Discharge criteria and follow-up
texts.body:
Criteria for discharge — all must be met
• Temperature <37.8°C on two consecutive observations ≥6 hours apart
• Heart rate <100 beats/min and respiratory rate <24 breaths/min
• Systolic blood pressure ≥90 mmHg
• SpO₂ ≥94% breathing air (or at the patient's documented home baseline)
• Able to take oral medication and tolerating diet and fluids
• Adequate community support and follow-up arrangements confirmed

Safety-net advice
Advise patients to return urgently if breathlessness worsens, temperature rises again, chest pain develops, or haemoptysis occurs. Provide written information on warning signs.

Follow-up
Arrange a follow-up chest X-ray at 6 weeks for patients who smoke, are aged ≥50 years, or have persisting symptoms, to exclude an underlying malignancy. Send a discharge summary to the GP documenting the organism identified (if any), the antibiotic course given, and allergy information recorded during the admission.

sets.title: Acute ischaemic stroke: hyperacute pathway
sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Stroke recognition & time windows
texts.body:
Community stroke recognition — FAST and ROSIER

FAST alert
• Face drooping (asymmetric smile or ptosis)
• Arm weakness (unable to raise one or both arms)
• Speech difficulties (slurred or absent)
• Time: call 999 immediately

ROSIER score (Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room)
Assign one point each for: asymmetric facial weakness; asymmetric arm weakness; asymmetric leg weakness; speech disturbance; visual field defect. Deduct one point for seizure at onset or loss of consciousness. A score of ≥1 predicts probable stroke.

Time windows
• Thrombolysis is eligible if onset is ≤4.5 hours ago (or last-known-well time is used if exact onset is unknown)
• Door-to-needle target: 60 minutes from hospital arrival
• Non-contrast CT head within 15 minutes of arrival for all hyperacute presentations
• Approximately 1.9 million neurones are lost per minute during proximal large vessel occlusion — time is brain.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Thrombolysis eligibility & contraindications
texts.body:
Thrombolysis eligibility — inclusion and exclusion

Inclusion criteria
• Confirmed ischaemic stroke with measurable neurological deficit
• Symptom onset ≤4.5 hours (or wake-up stroke with DWI–FLAIR mismatch on MRI)
• Age ≥18; no upper age limit in the absence of severe comorbidity

Absolute contraindications
• Prior intracranial haemorrhage at any time
• Stroke or significant head trauma within the preceding 3 months
• Major surgery or serious trauma within 14 days
• Platelet count <100×10⁹/L or INR >1.7
• DOAC taken within 48 hours unless levels confirmed as sub-therapeutic
• Uncontrolled hypertension: systolic BP >185 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg despite IV antihypertensive

Blood pressure eligibility
Systolic BP must be ≤185 mmHg and diastolic ≤110 mmHg before treatment commences. If targets cannot be achieved within 30 minutes, thrombolysis should be deferred.

Relative contraindications include pregnancy, recent lumbar puncture, and minor or rapidly improving neurological deficit.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Alteplase & tenecteplase dosing
texts.body:
Intravenous thrombolysis — drug dosing and monitoring

Alteplase
• Dose: 0.9 mg/kg IV, maximum total dose 90 mg
• Administration: give 10% of total dose as IV bolus over 1 minute, then infuse remainder over 60 minutes
• Do not exceed 90 mg regardless of body weight

Tenecteplase
• Dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV (maximum 25 mg) as a single intravenous bolus
• Preferred in centres with direct thrombectomy access; avoids prolonged infusion

Blood pressure targets
• Target BP <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after alteplase; treat excursions promptly with IV labetalol 10 mg or GTN infusion
• Check BP every 15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30 minutes for 23 hours

Antiplatelet and anticoagulant hold
Avoid antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy for 24 hours post-thrombolysis unless clinically indicated; restart only after review of 24-hour imaging.

Continuous cardiac monitoring and close neurological observation are required for 24 hours after treatment.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Mechanical thrombectomy & post-procedure care
texts.body:
Mechanical thrombectomy — eligibility and post-procedure care

Eligibility criteria
• Proximal large vessel occlusion (internal carotid artery, M1 segment of MCA, or basilar artery) confirmed on CT angiography
• NIHSS score ≥6
• ASPECTS score ≥6 on non-contrast CT, indicating adequate salvageable brain tissue
• Treatment feasible within 6 hours of onset; extended to 24 hours for patients with favourable perfusion mismatch on CT or MR perfusion imaging

Post-procedure monitoring
• NIHSS assessment every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then hourly until the patient is stable
• Blood pressure target: <160/90 mmHg after successful reperfusion
• 24-hour CT or MRI to assess reperfusion and exclude haemorrhagic transformation

Rehabilitation and nursing
• Dysphagia screening and early physiotherapy within 4 hours of admission
• Aspirin 300 mg once daily from day two unless thrombolysis was administered
• Nursing staff must document any new neurological deterioration immediately and escalate to the stroke team.

sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Diagnostic criteria and severity classification
texts.body:
Diagnostic triad
A diagnosis of DKA requires all three of the following:
• Blood glucose >11 mmol/L (or a confirmed diagnosis of diabetes mellitus)
• Blood ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L, or urine ketones 2+ or above on dipstick
• Bicarbonate <15 mmol/L and/or venous pH <7.3

Severity classification
Mild: venous pH 7.25–7.29; bicarbonate 15–17.9 mmol/L; patient alert and orientated.
Moderate: venous pH 7.0–7.24; bicarbonate <15 mmol/L.
Severe — any one of the following: venous pH <7.0; bicarbonate <5 mmol/L; Glasgow Coma Scale <12; SpO₂ <92% on air; systolic BP <90 mmHg; heart rate >100 or <60 bpm; anion gap >16 mmol/L.

Anion gap
Calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal range 12 ± 2 mmol/L. A raised anion gap alongside ketonaemia confirms a high anion gap metabolic acidosis typical of DKA.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Fixed-rate insulin infusion and fluid regimen
texts.body:
Fixed-rate insulin infusion (FRII)
Prescribe 0.1 units/kg/hour of soluble insulin made up in 0.9% sodium chloride. Do not stop or reduce the patient's usual background (basal) insulin while FRII is running.

Monitoring and dose adjustment
Check blood ketones and capillary glucose hourly. The target is a blood ketone fall of ≥0.5 mmol/L per hour. If ketones are not falling at this rate, increase the infusion rate by 1 unit/hour. Do not use a variable-rate insulin infusion (sliding scale) in DKA.

Glucose management
When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, add 10% glucose at 125 mL/hour alongside continuing 0.9% sodium chloride. Maintain blood glucose at 14–17 mmol/L until ketones have cleared.

Fluid replacement
Give 1 litre of 0.9% NaCl over the first hour, then reassess haemodynamic status and adjust subsequent bags accordingly.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Potassium replacement guide
texts.body:
Hypokalaemia is the most dangerous electrolyte complication of DKA treatment. Check serum potassium before starting the fixed-rate insulin infusion and do not commence FRII if K⁺ is below 3.5 mmol/L.

Replacement guide (per litre of IV fluid)
• K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L: do not add potassium to IV fluids; recheck after 1 hour
• K⁺ 3.5–5.5 mmol/L: add 40 mmol potassium chloride (KCl) per litre of IV fluid
• K⁺ <3.5 mmol/L: do not start insulin; seek urgent senior or critical care review; replace potassium more aggressively before proceeding

Monitoring frequency
In severe or moderate DKA: check serum potassium every hour for the first 4 hours, then every 2 hours thereafter. In mild DKA: check every 2 hours.

Caution
Never add more than 40 mmol KCl to a single 1-litre bag without senior authorisation. Hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >5.5 mmol/L) may worsen transiently as acidosis is corrected.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Resolution criteria, subcutaneous insulin transition and precipitant review
texts.body:
Resolution of DKA — all three criteria must be met
• Blood ketones <0.3 mmol/L
• Venous pH >7.3
• Bicarbonate >18 mmol/L
Blood glucose level alone is not a reliable marker of DKA resolution and must never be used as the sole criterion for stopping IV insulin.

Transition to subcutaneous insulin
Ensure the patient is eating and drinking normally before switching. Administer the patient's usual subcutaneous insulin dose, then wait 30–60 minutes before stopping the IV insulin infusion to prevent rebound ketosis. If the patient is newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, seek endocrinology advice before prescribing a subcutaneous regimen.

Precipitant review
Infection is the most common precipitant; send urine, blood cultures and a chest radiograph. Other precipitants include missed or insufficient insulin, new-onset type 1 diabetes, corticosteroids, antipsychotic drugs, and SGLT2 inhibitors (which can cause euglycaemic DKA even with near-normal glucose). Document the identified precipitant clearly in the discharge summary.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Severity classification and ECG changes
texts.body:
Severity bands (serum potassium)
• Mild: 5.5–5.9 mmol/L — often asymptomatic; dietary review and repeat U&E in 24–48 hours
• Moderate: 6.0–6.4 mmol/L — muscle weakness, nausea, palpitations possible; ECG and telemetry recommended
• Severe: ≥6.5 mmol/L — immediate treatment required; life-threatening arrhythmias possible

ECG changes (in order of severity)
• Peaked, symmetrical T waves — earliest change; typically appears above 5.5 mmol/L
• Prolonged PR interval and diminished P waves — appears above 6.0 mmol/L
• Widened QRS complex (>120 ms) — suggests K⁺ above 7.0 mmol/L; precedes ventricular arrhythmia
• Sine-wave pattern — K⁺ typically above 8.0 mmol/L; immediately pre-arrest

Pseudohyperkalaemia
Repeat a haemolysed sample before acting if the patient is clinically well and the ECG is normal. A second sample may show a falsely elevated result due to cell lysis in the tube.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Emergency drug treatment
texts.body:
Emergency treatment — drug sequence

Step 1 — Cardioprotection (first-line if ECG changes or K⁺ ≥6.5 mmol/L)
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 30 mL IV over 10 minutes; repeat after 5 minutes if ECG changes persist
• Onset: 1–3 minutes; duration: 30–60 minutes; does not lower serum potassium

Step 2 — Intracellular shift
• Actrapid (soluble insulin) 10 units IV with 25 g glucose (50 mL of 50% glucose); onset 15–30 minutes; lasts approximately 6 hours
• Monitor capillary glucose at 15 and 30 minutes after administration
• Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg as adjunct (avoid in ischaemic heart disease); onset approximately 30 minutes

Step 3 — Elimination
• Furosemide IV promotes kaliuresis when renal function is adequate
• Patiromer or sodium polystyrene sulphonate (Resonium) orally; potassium-binding resins act over hours
• Haemodialysis if refractory or renal failure

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Common causes and medication review
texts.body:
Common causes
Renal
• Acute kidney injury (AKI) or chronic kidney disease (CKD): impaired urinary potassium excretion
• Adrenal insufficiency or hypoaldosteronism: reduced distal tubule K⁺ secretion

Drug-induced (review and withhold acutely)
• ACE inhibitors and ARBs (e.g. ramipril, losartan): inhibit aldosterone production; commonest iatrogenic cause
• Potassium-sparing diuretics: spironolactone, amiloride, eplerenone
• NSAIDs: impair renal prostaglandins and reduce kaliuresis
• Trimethoprim at high doses: blocks distal K⁺ secretion
• Heparin and LMWH: suppress aldosterone synthesis
• Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin): impair tubular K⁺ excretion

Other causes
• Metabolic acidosis: transcellular shift moves K⁺ out of cells into plasma
• Rhabdomyolysis, major haemolysis, or massive blood transfusion: release intracellular K⁺
• Excess dietary intake in CKD

Medication review
Withhold the offending drug acutely; restart only once K⁺ is below 5.5 mmol/L and a senior clinician has reviewed the indication.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Monitoring and escalation criteria
texts.body:
Monitoring frequency
• Mild (5.5–5.9 mmol/L): repeat U&E in 24–48 hours; telemetry not required unless symptomatic
• Moderate (6.0–6.4 mmol/L): repeat U&E and ECG at 2 hours; continuous telemetry for at least 4 hours
• Severe (≥6.5 mmol/L): continuous cardiac monitoring; recheck U&E at 1 hour and 4 hours post-treatment

Post-insulin glucose monitoring
Hypoglycaemia occurs in up to 10% of patients; check blood glucose at 15, 30, and 60 minutes after the insulin–glucose dose and treat any reading below 4.0 mmol/L promptly.

Involve the renal team if
• K⁺ remains ≥6.0 mmol/L after two treatment rounds
• CKD stage 4–5, new AKI not responding to IV fluids, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours

Involve ICU or HDU if
• Cardiac arrest, refractory K⁺ ≥7.0 mmol/L, or haemodynamic instability requiring immediate haemodialysis

sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Severity classification
texts.body:
Acute asthma severity is graded into four categories using clinical signs and physiological measurements.

Moderate acute asthma
• PEF 50–75% of personal best or predicted
• No features listed below; sentences completed without distress

Severe acute asthma — any ONE of:
• PEF 33–50% of best or predicted
• Respiratory rate ≥ 25 breaths/min
• Heart rate ≥ 110 beats/min
• Inability to complete sentences in one breath

Life-threatening asthma — any ONE of:
• PEF < 33% of best or predicted
• SpO₂ < 92% on any oxygen
• PaO₂ < 8 kPa on air or supplemental oxygen
• Silent chest, cyanosis, or feeble respiratory effort
• Bradycardia, hypotension, or dysrhythmia
• Confusion, exhaustion, or depressed consciousness

Near-fatal asthma: raised PaCO₂ (≥ 6 kPa) and/or requirement for mechanical ventilation indicating severe respiratory fatigue.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Initial treatment
texts.body:
Oxygen
Target SpO₂ 94–98% using controlled supplemental oxygen; avoid hyperoxia. In life-threatening presentations, ensure ≥ 94% is maintained continuously.

Bronchodilators
• Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised; repeat every 15–30 minutes or more frequently in the first hour if needed, then guided by clinical response
• Ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg nebulised every 4–6 hours; add to salbutamol in all severe or life-threatening presentations
• Back-to-back nebulisers may be administered in the most severe cases

Corticosteroids
• Prednisolone 40–50 mg orally once daily; continue for at least 5 days or until full recovery
• If oral route not tolerated: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily

IV magnesium sulphate
• Magnesium sulphate 1.2–2 g intravenously over 20 minutes for life-threatening asthma or severe asthma poorly responding to initial bronchodilator therapy
• Give as a single dose; routine repetition is not recommended

texts.label: C
texts.heading: ICU referral criteria and arterial blood gas indications
texts.body:
Perform an arterial blood gas (ABG) in any patient with:
• SpO₂ < 92% on initial assessment
• Life-threatening features present at any point
• Failure to improve within 15–30 minutes of initial treatment
• PEF remaining below 50% after one hour of treatment

Interpreting results
• Normal or rising PaCO₂ in a breathless, distressed patient is an ominous sign; escalate without delay
• PaO₂ < 8 kPa despite supplemental oxygen indicates severe hypoxaemia
• pH < 7.35 or falling pH suggests respiratory fatigue and impending failure

Criteria for immediate ICU or HDU referral
• Requirement for non-invasive ventilation or endotracheal intubation
• PaCO₂ rising despite maximal medical therapy
• Deteriorating consciousness or progressive exhaustion
• Cardiorespiratory arrest or peri-arrest situation

Involve the ICU team early; a senior review must not be deferred until the patient is moribund.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Discharge criteria, follow-up, and inhaler technique
texts.body:
Before discharge, ALL of the following criteria must be satisfied:
• PEF ≥ 75% of personal best or predicted, sustained for at least 1 hour
• Diurnal PEF variability < 25%
• SpO₂ ≥ 94% on air
• Symptoms well controlled on the proposed discharge regimen
• No nocturnal waking or wheeze the night before discharge

Inhaler technique
Assess and document inhaler technique at every discharge. A spacer device must be issued whenever a pressurised metered-dose inhaler is prescribed, as it significantly improves lower airway deposition. Correct sequence: shake canister, exhale fully, seal lips around mouthpiece, depress canister, inhale slowly and deeply, then hold breath for 10 seconds.

Follow-up
• Primary care or asthma nurse review within 2 working days of discharge
• Respiratory outpatient appointment within 4 weeks
• Provide a written self-management plan at discharge, including escalation criteria and when to call emergency services

sets.instruction: Look at Texts A–D. Questions 1–7: which text? Questions 8–15: word/short phrase from the texts. Questions 16–20: complete the sentence. Spelling matters. Target: 15 minutes.

texts.label: A
texts.heading: Recognition criteria and differential diagnosis
texts.body:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening generalised hypersensitivity reaction. The UK Resuscitation Council criteria require all three of the following: sudden onset with rapid progression of symptoms; life-threatening airway, breathing, or circulation problems; and skin or mucosal changes (urticaria, flushing, angioedema) — though skin signs may be absent in up to 20% of cases.

System-specific features
• Airway: stridor, hoarseness, tongue or throat swelling
• Breathing: acute bronchospasm, wheeze, tachypnoea, SpO₂ <94%
• Circulation: hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or >30% fall from baseline), tachycardia, pallor, syncope

Differential diagnoses
• Vasovagal syncope: brief loss of consciousness, bradycardia, no urticaria
• Asthma exacerbation: bronchospasm without systemic features
• Hereditary angioedema (HAE): swelling without urticaria; does not respond to adrenaline
• Carcinoid syndrome: episodic flushing without allergen trigger

Risk is higher with parenteral allergen exposure (IV drugs, insect stings) than with oral ingestion.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Adrenaline dosing: route, dose and repeat interval
texts.body:
Adrenaline 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) by intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

IM doses
• Adult and child >12 years: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
• Child 6–12 years: 300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
• Child 6 months–6 years: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
• Child <6 months: 100–150 micrograms (0.1–0.15 mL)

Repeat dose: if no improvement after 5 minutes, administer a further IM dose at the same volume.

Auto-injectors
The standard adult auto-injector (EpiPen 0.3 mg, Jext 300 micrograms, Emerade 300 micrograms) delivers 300 micrograms; the junior auto-injector (EpiPen Jr 0.15 mg, Jext 150 micrograms) delivers 150 micrograms. Check the expiry date before prescribing.

IV route: use only in a specialist setting with continuous cardiac monitoring; adult bolus dose is 50 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1:10,000 solution), titrated cautiously.

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Refractory anaphylaxis: IV infusion and adjunct therapy
texts.body:
Refractory anaphylaxis is defined as failure to respond after two or more doses of IM adrenaline. Immediate escalation to IV adrenaline infusion with ICU involvement is required.

IV adrenaline infusion preparation
Dilute 1 mg adrenaline in 100 mL sodium chloride 0.9% to give a concentration of 10 micrograms/mL. Start at 0.05 micrograms/kg/minute and titrate to clinical response.

Fluid resuscitation
Anaphylaxis causes massive vasodilation and capillary leak. Give 500 mL–1 L crystalloid IV over 5–10 minutes; repeat boluses as required. Colloids are not recommended over crystalloids.

Second-line adjuncts (after adrenaline)
• Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV — H1 antihistamine; reduces urticaria but does not reverse hypotension
• Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV — slow onset; may attenuate biphasic reactions
• Glucagon 1–2 mg IV — for patients on beta-blockers unresponsive to adrenaline

Refractory bronchospasm: nebulised salbutamol 5 mg; consider IV magnesium sulphate 1.2–2 g over 20 minutes.

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Observation periods, mast cell tryptase and discharge
texts.body:
Observation periods
• All patients: minimum 4 hours after symptom onset before any discharge decision
• Severe reaction (respiratory compromise, hypotension, or loss of consciousness) or known biphasic risk factors: 12–24 hours inpatient observation

Mast cell tryptase sampling
• Sample 1: as soon as possible (ideally within 1 hour of onset)
• Sample 2: at 1–2 hours after onset (peak level)
• Sample 3 (baseline): at ≥24 hours after the reaction or on recovery
A result exceeding 1.2× baseline + 2 ng/mL supports the diagnosis of anaphylaxis.

Discharge requirements — ALL must be met
• Prescribe and demonstrate two adrenaline auto-injectors; confirm patient and carer competence
• Provide a written anaphylaxis action plan
• Advise patient to wear medical alert identification
• Arrange allergy referral within 1 week and specialist clinic follow-up within 4–6 weeks
• Document the identified trigger in the discharge letter

texts.label: A
texts.heading: AKI definition and KDIGO staging criteria
texts.body:
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined as any of:
• Rise in serum creatinine ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours
• Rise in serum creatinine to ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days
• Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 consecutive hours

KDIGO staging
• Stage 1: creatinine 1.5–1.9× baseline OR rise ≥26.5 µmol/L; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours
• Stage 2: creatinine 2.0–2.9× baseline; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 hours
• Stage 3: creatinine ≥3× baseline OR ≥353.6 µmol/L with acute rise ≥26.5 µmol/L; urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 hours OR anuria for ≥12 hours; or initiation of renal replacement therapy

AKI staging guides escalation of monitoring and therapy intensity. Document baseline creatinine using the lowest value within the preceding 3 months.

texts.label: B
texts.heading: Common causes and risk factors for AKI
texts.body:
Pre-renal (reduced perfusion)
• Hypovolaemia: diarrhoea, vomiting, haemorrhage, inadequate fluid intake
• Sepsis and distributive shock
• Cardiac failure with low output state
• Hepatorenal syndrome

Intrinsic renal
• Acute tubular necrosis (ATN): most common; caused by ischaemia or nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast media, NSAIDs, vancomycin)
• Acute interstitial nephritis: often drug-induced (penicillins, NSAIDs, PPIs) or immune-mediated
• Glomerulonephritis: proteinuria and haematuria on urinalysis raises suspicion

Post-renal (obstruction)
• Bladder outlet obstruction (enlarged prostate, neurogenic bladder)
• Bilateral ureteric obstruction (pelvic malignancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis)

High-risk groups
• Age ≥65 years
• Chronic kidney disease (CKD): baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m²
• Diabetes, heart failure, liver disease
• Recent nephrotoxin exposure (contrast, aminoglycosides, NSAIDs)

texts.label: C
texts.heading: Immediate AKI management bundle
texts.body:
Assess and act within 6 hours of AKI recognition.

Fluid resuscitation
• Give 500 mL crystalloid bolus (e.g. Hartmann's solution or 0.9% sodium chloride) if hypovolaemic; reassess after each bolus
• Avoid aggressive fluid loading in AKI secondary to cardiac failure; seek senior advice

Stop nephrotoxins
• Withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and diuretics when AKI is confirmed unless specifically indicated
• Withhold aminoglycosides; if aminoglycosides essential, use once-daily dosing with serum level monitoring

Monitoring
• Urinalysis: dipstick for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites; send urine for microscopy and culture
• Strict fluid balance with hourly urine output monitoring; insert catheter if output uncertain
• Renal ultrasound within 24 hours to exclude obstruction if cause unclear

Escalation
• Serum creatinine, electrolytes, and bicarbonate every 6–12 hours in Stage 2–3 AKI

texts.label: D
texts.heading: Renal referral, dialysis indications, and drug dosing
texts.body:
Indications for urgent renal team review
• Suspected glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, or interstitial nephritis
• AKI with no identifiable cause following initial assessment
• Stage 3 AKI or AKI on CKD with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²
• Refractory hyperkalaemia: K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L despite medical treatment
• Severe metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate <15 mmol/L
• Fluid overload refractory to diuretics

Renal replacement therapy (RRT) triggers
RRT is considered when any of: hyperkalaemia unresponsive to treatment, uraemic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or severe pulmonary oedema not responsive to diuretics.

Drug dosing in AKI
• Low-molecular-weight heparin: reduce dose or switch to unfractionated heparin when eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²
• Metformin: withhold in all stages of AKI
• Renally cleared antibiotics (e.g. trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin): withhold or adjust; seek pharmacy advice
